title: Women scholars today
hook: women teaching fiqh, hadith and Qur'an across the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, scholarship today: Cairo, Najaf, Qom, Deoband, Medina, and a laptop on a kitchen table. Your line was where they study. Which place did you look up? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

A group of women in Medina has a complaint, and they bring it straight to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The men, they say, are always around you. They get all your time. So give us a day of our own. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and what happens next is simple. He agrees. He promises them a day, meets them on it, and teaches them. No one in the report tells them to wait for their husbands to pass the lessons on. They asked for a teacher, and they got one. Today: the women who learn, and the women who teach.
screen: `THE MEN GET ALL YOUR TIME.` → `GIVE US A DAY.` → `HE AGREES, AND TEACHES THEM.`

segments.voice: Begin with the Qur'an, which speaks to women and men side by side. In Pickthall's translation, one verse runs: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe," and it goes on, pair after pair, the truthful, the patient, the humble, the fasting, the ones who remember Allah, and promises all of them forgiveness and a reward. Then the women who asked for a day. They didn't treat knowledge as something that would trickle down to them. They went to the source. Tradition says the companions brought their questions to a woman too: 'Aisha, the Prophet's wife. Al-Bukhari's collection carries her reports, and in some of them she corrects what others had passed on, as when she answers a report about the dead and the weeping of their families. Tradition remembers women after her too, women who taught hadith and law in their own cities, and whose names stand in the chains of transmission alongside men's. One of them, Karima of Merv, is remembered for teaching Sahih al-Bukhari itself. So what does it look like today? Women teach the Qur'an and its recitation, women teach hadith, women teach fiqh, the law of daily life, in mosques, in seminaries and colleges, in living rooms and online classes. Communities and schools of thought hold different views on how and where women should teach, and to whom, and those views are held seriously. But the line from the hook still runs: a group of women asking for a teacher, and a Prophet who set the day.
screen: `MEN AND WOMEN, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THEY WENT TO THE SOURCE.` · `'AISHA SETS THE RECORD STRAIGHT.` · `WOMEN IN THE CHAINS, THEN AND NOW.` · then, large: `SHE TEACHES.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember a woman who taught you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who taught you something that stuck. A mother, a grandmother, a teacher in school, an aunt in a kitchen, a neighbor who knew things. Picture her face as she explained it. What did she know that you didn't? Thank her, in your head, for a moment. If you pray, you can remember her in your prayers. Then, after the bell, set yourself one small task: learn the name of one woman, today or in history, who teaches the Qur'an, hadith or law. The bell holds the time.
Women scholars today. Women teaching Qur'an, hadith and the law of daily life, in a line that runs back to 'Aisha and the women who asked for a day. Today's word.
Your line: she teaches. Today, learn one woman scholar's name, from history or from now, and one thing she taught. Tomorrow, art and music debates. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Muslim women study and teach Qur'an recitation, hadith and fiqh in mosques, seminaries, universities and online, and communities differ on the settings in which women teach.

what it means: women asked the Prophet for their own day of teaching, 'Aisha corrected what others had passed on, and women teach Qur'an, hadith and fiqh today.
what a scholar hears: the women's day in Sahih al-Bukhari, 'Aisha's corrections, and women in the isnad, the chains of transmission, such as Karima al-Marwaziyya.

notes: Confirm Bukhari 101 and Pickthall's exact wording of the opening of 33:35.
'The companions themselves went to a woman with their questions' should be backed by a specific report a Keeper can cite.
'In some of them she corrects what others had passed on' needs a specific example cited by a Keeper (e.g., her responses on the dead being punished for the weeping of relatives).
Karima al-Marwaziyya (of Merv) is introduced with 'the story goes' and 'tradition remembers'; confirm the description as a transmitter of Sahih al-Bukhari.
No modern women scholars are named, to avoid unverified claims about living people; the practice asks the listener to learn a name. A Keeper may add one or two names.
The differing views on where and to whom women teach are mentioned without detail or ranking; confirm the phrasing.

Editor: 'the companions went to 'Aisha with their questions' is now 'tradition says' and no longer drives the screen, match or trapdoor; her correction is tied to a cited report (Bukhari 1288, confirm number); the garbled Karima line was rewritten, and the match pair 'a teacher of al-Bukhari' (which read as teaching the man himself) now says 'teaching Sahih al-Bukhari'.
